{{Short description|none}} {{Use dmy dates|date=January 2026}} {{Use New Zealand English|date=May 2023}} {{Infobox political party | name = Alliance | logo = File:NZ Alliance logo 2025.svg | logo_size = 250 | founder = [[Jim Anderton]] | foundation = 1 December 1991 | ideology = {{ubl|class=nowrap| |[[Democratic socialism]]{{cite web|title=About us|url=http://alliance.org.nz/about/|publisher=Alliance|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714210843/http://alliance.org.nz/about/|archive-date=14 July 2014|date=29 April 2008|quote=The Alliance is a broad inclusive party of the Left with policies based on democratic socialist principles: democracy, equality and social ownership.}}{{cite web|title=New Zealand: Alliance adopts a socialist manifesto |work=[[Green Left Weekly]] |url=https://www.greenleft.org.au/content/new-zealand-alliance-adopts-socialist-manifesto |publisher=Green Left Association |access-date=12 November 2016|date=14 January 2004}}{{efn|The Alliance, in its first incarnation, followed a social democratic ideology from 1991 to 2002.}} }} | youth_wing = Staunch Alliance (defunct) | position = [[Left-wing politics|Left-wing]]{{efn|The Alliance had centre and centre-left factions from 1991 to 2002.}} | colours = {{color box|#8B181A|border=darkgray}} [[Red]]
{{color box|#106D5F|border=darkgray}} [[Teal]] | website = {{URL|https://allianceparty.nz/}} | country = New Zealand | affiliation1_title = Members (pre-2002) | affiliation1 = {{ubl|class=nowrap|[[New Zealand Democratic Party|Democratic Party]]|[[Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand|Green Party]]|[[Mana Motuhake]]|[[NewLabour Party (New Zealand)|NewLabour Party]]|[[New Zealand Liberal Party (1991)|Liberal Party]]}} | colorcode = {{party color|Alliance (New Zealand political party)}} | leader = [[Victor Billot]] | president = Tom Roud }} The '''Alliance''' is a [[Left-wing politics|left-wing]] [[List of political parties in New Zealand|political party in New Zealand]]. It was formed at the end of 1991 by the linking of four smaller parties. The Alliance positions itself as a [[democratic socialist]] alternative to the [[centre-left politics|centre-left]] [[New Zealand Labour Party]]. It was influential throughout the 1990s, but suffered a major setback after its founder and leader, [[Jim Anderton]], left the party in 2002, taking with him several of its [[members of parliament]] (MPs). After the remaining MPs lost their seats in the [[2002 New Zealand general election|2002 general election]], some commentators predicted the demise of the party. The Alliance stood candidates in the [[2005 New Zealand general election|2005 general election]] but won less than 1% of the party vote. It contested [[Auckland City Council]] elections under the [[City Vision (Auckland, New Zealand political ticket)|City Vision]] banner, in concert with the New Zealand Labour Party and Green Party. The Alliance ran 15 electorate candidates and a total of 30 candidates on the party list in the [[2008 New Zealand general election|2008 general election]], increasing its party vote marginally from that in 2005. It was deregistered at its own request in 2015, though the party never formally dissolved.{{cite web |url=http://www.elections.org.nz/news-media/amendments-register-political-parties-2 |title=Amendments to the Register of Political Parties |publisher=Electoral Commission |date=26 May 2015 |access-date=27 May 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150527063600/http://www.elections.org.nz/news-media/amendments-register-political-parties-2 |archive-date=27 May 2015 |url-status=dead }}{{cite web|title=Alliance Party deregistered |url=http://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/68904981/alliance-party-deregistered |website=Stuff |access-date=12 November 2016|date=27 May 2015}} On 1 June 2025 the party announced its relaunch to stand a candidate in the [[2025 New Zealand local elections]]. On 21 January 2026 the Alliance announced it will be standing electorate candidates across the country in the [[2026 New Zealand general election]].{{cite web|title=We are back to fight for working people in 2026|url=https://allianceparty.nz/we-are-back-to-fight-for-working-people-in-2026/ |website= Alliance Party website |access-date= 27 January 2026|date=21 January 2026}} It was re-registered in August 2026. ==History== {{More citations needed section|date=October 2026}} ===Foundation=== The Alliance was formed at the end of 1991 as an alliance of four parties.{{cite web |last1=Curtin |first1=Jennifer |last2=Miller |first2=Raymond |author1-link=Jennifer Curtin |title=Small parties in the 1990s |url=https://teara.govt.nz/en/political-parties/page-5 |website=[[Te Ara: The Encyclopedia of New Zealand]] |access-date=4 June 2022 |language=en-NZ |date=21 July 2015}} The largest of the four was the [[NewLabour Party (New Zealand)|NewLabour Party]] (not associated with the later [[New Labour]] movement in the UK), established by former [[New Zealand Labour Party|Labour Party]] politician [[Jim Anderton]]. The oldest was the [[New Zealand Democratic Party|Democratic Party]] (originally known as the [[Social Credit Party (New Zealand)|Social Credit Political League]], and dedicated to [[Social Credit]] policies). The others were [[Mana Motuhake (political party)|Mana Motuhake]] (a Māori party) and the [[Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand|Greens]] (an environmentalist party).{{cite news |title=Alliance born with eye on Tamaki win |author=Orsman, Bernard |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=2 December 1991 |page=1 }}{{sfn|Casey|2002|p=101}} Until his departure from Labour in 1989, Anderton had been the most vocal Labour MP in his criticism of his party's new direction. Led by [[Roger Douglas]], the [[Minister of Finance (New Zealand)|Minister of Finance]], Labour had adopted radical policies of economic liberalisation, [[free trade]], and privatisation of state assets – sharply in contrast both with the party's background and its campaign promises. This was deeply unpopular both with a section of the public and with ordinary members, but Douglas and his allies, without effective constraint by [[Prime Minister of New Zealand|Prime Minister]] [[David Lange]], pressed on with the reforms. Anderton, despite heavy pressure from the party authorities, refused to vote in favour of the measures, and eventually quit the party. He contested the [[1990 New Zealand general election|1990 election]] under the banner of NewLabour, a party he quickly established. He successfully retained his electorate seat, becoming the first MP to leave a party and not lose their position in the next elections. NewLabour, the Democrats, and Mana Motuhake, all of which opposed the platform set out by Douglas, gradually began to work together to fight their common political opposition. The Greens, who had policies and electoral support, but not party organisation, also took notice. Initially, this co-operation was limited, but expanded after a joint candidate was successful in an [[Auckland]] local-body election. In two concurrent by-elections on the [[Auckland Regional Council]] (ARC) in November 1991 the parties coalesced around a single candidate in each race; [[Bruce Jesson]] of NewLabour in the Panmure Ward and Ruth Norman from the Greens in the Glenfield Ward. Both were successful giving a huge boost in confidence and publicity to the incipient party.{{cite news |title=Voters go for new parties |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=28 November 1991 |page=1 }} [[File:NewZealandAlliancePartyLogo-Old.png|thumb|Original party logo]] On 1 December 1991, NewLabour, the Greens, the Democrats, and Mana Motuhake formally agreed to establish the Alliance as an official party. This established the three original pillars of Alliance policy – left-wing economics (represented by NewLabour and the Democrats), environmentalism (represented by the Greens), and Māori issues (represented by Mana Motuhake). Shortly after the official establishment of the Alliance, a small splinter group from the [[New Zealand National Party|National Party]] applied to join. This group, known as the [[New Zealand Liberal Party (1991)|Liberal Party]] (not to be confused with the [[New Zealand Liberal Party|original Liberal Party]]), consisted of two former National Party MPs who were disillusioned with the continuation of Douglas's policies by National's [[Ruth Richardson]]. The Liberals became the fifth member of the Alliance in June 1992. The addition of the two Liberal MPs ([[Gilbert Myles]] and [[Hamish MacIntyre]]) together with Anderton gave the party more of a presence in parliament.{{cite news |title=Alliance caucus triples power |author=Murphy, Tim |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=8 June 1992 |page=2 }} Later at the Alliance's inaugural party conference in November 1992 Anderton was officially confirmed as party leader and members elected [[Sandra Lee-Vercoe|Sandra Lee]] of Mana Motuhake and [[Jeanette Fitzsimons]] from the Greens as co-deputy leaders.{{cite news |title=Alliance gets three-way leadership |author=Laugesen, Ruth |work=[[The Dominion (Wellington)|The Dominion]] |date=16 November 1992 |page=2 }} There were also discussions regarding the Alliance's links with [[Winston Peters]], a former National MP who founded the [[New Zealand First]] party. Peters was also opposed to the economic reforms being undertaken, was hostile towards big business, and claimed to support ordinary New Zealanders, but was also highly [[Conservatism|conservative]] in his social policies. In particular, his views on [[immigration]] were incompatible with the Alliance's belief in multiculturalism. There were also problems regarding who would lead any merged entity – both the Alliance's Anderton and New Zealand First's Peters were well regarded for standing up to their old parties, leaving it unclear which of them should be senior. (Some have also claimed that neither Anderton nor Peters would accept being ranked second – both politicians are sometimes accused by their critics of being egotistical and controlling). Regardless of the reason, the Alliance and New Zealand First did not move together. As a result, Myles and several other top figures in the Liberal Party left the Alliance and joined with New Zealand First instead.{{cite news |author=Orsman, Bernard |title=Myles and Alliance trade jibes |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |page=2 |date=17 July 1993 }} ===Early electoral performance=== In 1992, the Alliance [[1992 Tamaki by-election|contested a by-election]] in the electorate of [[Tāmaki (New Zealand electorate)|Tamaki]]. The former stronghold of [[Robert Muldoon]], a former National Party prime minister, Tamaki was not regarded as an easy run for the Alliance. It was, therefore, surprising when the Alliance nearly took the seat off National after going to first place in several polls. The Alliance candidate, [[Chris Leitch (politician)|Chris Leitch]] of the Democrats, finished a close second behind National's [[Clem Simich]], pushing Labour into third place.{{cite news |title=Miracle just fails Leitch |author=Rapson, Bevan |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=17 February 1992 |page=1 }} In February 1992 the Alliance won a third by-election on the ARC when [[Mike Lee (New Zealand politician)|Mike Lee]] of NewLabour won the Auckland Central Ward giving the party further momentum.{{cite news |title=Alliance scoops byelection vote |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=20 February 1992 |page=1 }} Later that year, the Alliance made further gains in the 1992 local-body elections campaigning on a platform of halting the sale of public utilities. After a strong campaign the party gained control of the ARC's services trust and was able to cease sales.{{cite news |title=Sale stance vindicated — Alliance |author=Townsend, Kevin |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=12 October 1992 |page=3 }} These two performances helped establish the Alliance as a significant threat to the major parties. In the [[1993 New Zealand general election|1993 election]], the Alliance gained 18% of the vote. However, the electoral system meant that the party only won two seats – one delivered by Jim Anderton, and the other by [[Sandra Lee-Vercoe|Sandra Lee]] in Auckland. Occurring at the same time as this election, however, was the referendum which introduced the [[Mixed-member proportional representation|mixed-member proportional]] (MMP) representation electoral system, making it much easier for smaller parties to get representation. The Alliance was a strong supporter of this change. In 1994, Jim Anderton left the leadership of the Alliance, citing family reasons. Sandra Lee was placed in charge of the party. Later, however, Anderton was persuaded to return, and resumed the leadership.{{cite news |title=Anderton back at top for long haul |author=Young, Audrey |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=8 May 1995 |page=1 }} ===Under MMP=== In the [[1996 New Zealand general election|1996 election]], the Alliance gained 10% of the vote. Under the new electoral system, this secured the party thirteen MPs.{{cite web |url= https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_1996/pdf/1.1%20Summary%20of%20overall%20results.pdf |title=1996 election summary of official results |publisher=[[New Zealand Electoral Commission]] |access-date=19 May 2018 }} New Zealand First, however, had obtained seventeen MPs, and held the balance of power between Labour and National. Eventually, New Zealand First leader Winston Peters opted to form a coalition with National, leaving both Labour and the Alliance in opposition. The Labour Party, now led by [[Helen Clark]], had moved away from the policies of Roger Douglas — both Douglas and his strongest supporter, [[Richard Prebble]], had left Labour to found the [[ACT New Zealand|ACT]] party, and Clark's more traditional faction had taken over. This allowed a gradual reconciliation between Labour and the Alliance, a process assisted by the impression that lack of cooperation had cost both parties support. Eventually, this led to an agreement between the two parties in 1998, with both sides agreeing to cooperate in forming a government should election results allow it. In 1997, the Greens decided that they would leave the Alliance at the next election, believing that they could perform better individually.{{cite web |url=http://greens.org.nz/about/history.htm |title=Greens in Time and Space: The History of The Green Party 1972–1999 |author=Christine Dann |publisher=Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand |access-date=18 May 2018 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081010175959/http://www.greens.org.nz/about/history.htm |archive-date=10 October 2008 }} However, MP Philida Bunkle left the Greens to remain with the Alliance. Other developments in the Alliance's makeup included the formal dissolution of both the NewLabour Party and the Liberal Party, with their members becoming members of the Alliance as a whole rather than of any specific constituent party. This left the Democrats and Mana Motuhake as the only parts of the Alliance with distinct identities. In the [[1999 New Zealand general election|1999 election]], the Alliance gained around 8% of the vote, giving it ten seats. This, combined with Labour's forty-nine seats and some support from the Greens, was enough to form a coalition government.{{cite web |url=https://www.parliament.nz/resource/en-nz/00PLLawRP99111/4d5c2cf501956d02710301e0b3284ae8bc5758f7 |title=Final results update for the 1999 New Zealand general election |publisher=New Zealand Parliament Library |date=23 December 1999 |access-date=18 May 2018 }} Jim Anderton became [[Deputy Prime Minister of New Zealand|Deputy Prime Minister]], and three other Alliance MPs gained positions in [[Cabinet of New Zealand|Cabinet]]. The Alliance claims to have made a number of significant achievements while in government, citing (among other things) the creation of the [[Ministry of Economic Development (New Zealand)|Ministry of Economic Development]], the lifting of the [[minimum wage]], a change in funding systems for schools, and abolition of market rents for [[State housing in New Zealand|state housing]]. The party also claims to have exerted an important general influence over other governmental decisions. ===Split=== Towards the end of the parliamentary term, however, internal tensions began to grow within the Alliance. This was partly driven by the party's low poll ratings, which were often blamed on perceived "subservience" to Labour. In particular, many members of the party organisation were less willing to support Labour than the party's MPs were, leading to a rift between parliamentary leader Anderton and party president [[Matt McCarten]]. On 3 April 2002, Anderton and Lee announced they would not stand for the Alliance in the next general election.{{Cite press release |date=3 April 2002 |title=Anderton's News Conference On Alliance Split |url= https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PA0204/S00049/andertons-news-conference-on-alliance-split.htm |publisher=Alliance Party |access-date=6 June 2024 |agency=Scoop News}} However, rules regarding changes of party allegiance meant that Anderton and his allies could not officially resign from the Alliance without also resigning from parliament, leading to the awkward situation of Anderton and his allies technically remaining part of the Alliance while actually operating outside of it. Anderton, along with the Democrats (with MPs Grant Gillon and John Wright) and Matt Robson (formerly of NewLabour), established the Progressive Coalition Party (later just the [[New Zealand Progressive Party|Progressive Party]]). [[Laila Harré]] became the leader of the remaining Alliance, supported by MPs Willie Jackson and Liz Gordon. The rest of Mana Motuhake also stayed with the Alliance. The remaining three MPs (Bunkle and Lee supporting Anderton and Kevin Campbell supporting Harré) decided not to stand for parliament again. Labour was largely successful in avoiding being drawn into the dispute. The conflict within the Alliance was one of the reasons cited by Helen Clark for her calling the election several months early in 2002. ===Decline=== In the [[2002 New Zealand general election|2002 election]], the Alliance and the Progressives competed against each other. The Alliance, believing that it would struggle to reach 5% (the threshold for a party being awarded representation proportional to its support), needed to win an electorate seat to gain entry to parliament. It chose to focus on {{NZ electorate link|Waitakere}} (contested by Harré) and {{NZ electorate link|Tainui}} (contested by [[Willie Jackson (politician)|Willie Jackson]], leader of Mana Motuhake). In both seats, however, the Alliance came second, losing each time to a Labour candidate, and so failed to gain parliamentary representation. In the list vote, the party failed to meet the threshold, gaining only 1.27% of the Party vote.{{cite web |title=Official Count Results – Overall Status |url= http://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2002/partystatus.html |publisher=Electoral Commission |access-date=7 August 2013}} After the election, Mana Motuhake chose to leave the Alliance (the Democrats also choosing to leave the newly launched Progressive Coalition at the same time).{{Cite web |date=28 June 2025 |title=Go-it-alone spirit spurs final split from Alliance |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/go-it-alone-spirit-spurs-final-split-from-alliance/WIJCCFRGONU2KJTVHFYHTF5WCA/ |access-date=28 June 2025 |website=NZ Herald |language=en-NZ}} This left the Alliance without any component parties – all members were now simply members of the Alliance as a whole. [[File:NewZealandAlliancePartyLogo.png|thumb|2003 logo]] Laila Harré stepped down as the party's leader on 30 November 2003, and was replaced by [[Matt McCarten]], the party president who clashed with Anderton. McCarten advocated a policy which would see the Alliance focus less on electoral activity and more on playing a co-ordinating role—he has been a particularly strong advocate of working with the new [[Māori Party]], which the Alliance had been involved with and practically supported during Tariana Turia's by-election campaign and the Maori Party launch. There was a debate within the Alliance, given the poll ratings of less than 1%, as to whether the Alliance should contest the list vote in the [[2005 New Zealand general election|2005 election]], or instead only stand in electorate seats and encourage its supporters to use their list vote to support the [[Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand|Greens]] or the Māori Party. [[Jill Ovens]], a former candidate and the new party president, was critical of McCarten's support of the Māori Party, saying that working both for the Alliance and the Māori Party at the same time represented a conflict of interest and resigned at one stage over the issue (Ovens subsequently joined the Labour Party in 2006). When no agreement could be reached on the electoral strategy McCarten and Harré disassociated themselves from the Alliance. Gerard Hehir, the outgoing General Secretary, informed the Electoral Commission that the Alliance no longer had the five hundred financial members required for registration. In late 2004 McCarten was replaced as leader by two co-leaders, Jill Ovens and [[Paul Piesse]] and the party's remaining membership voted to contest the list vote.{{cite web |url=http://www.alliance.org.nz/info.php3?Type=Media&ID=1808 |title=Alliance New Zealand |website=www.alliance.org.nz |access-date=17 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20041215000257/http://www.alliance.org.nz/info.php3?Type=Media&ID=1808 |archive-date=15 December 2004 |url-status=dead}} In the 2005 election, the Alliance gained only 0.07% of the Party vote, placing 12th of the parties. [[File:Alliance candidates for the 2008 election.jpg|thumb|Alliance candidates for the [[2008 New Zealand general election|2008 election]]: Andrew McKenzie (number two on the [[Party lists in the 2008 New Zealand general election#Alliance|party list]]), Victor Billot (number three), Sarita Divis (number nine) and Kay Murray (number one)]] Following its poor showing in the 2005 election, the Alliance continued after their 2005 conference with two co-leaders [[Paul Piesse]] and Len Richards. At the 2006 conference held in Wellington, no co-leaders were elected with the party deciding to concentrate on internal reorganisation. [[Victor Billot]] was elected president. At the 2007 national conference, held in Dunedin, two co-leaders were elected, [[Victor Billot]] and [[Kay Murray]], with [[Paul Piesse]] returning to his former role as Party President. Speakers at the 2007 national conference included political commentator [[Chris Trotter]] and publisher [[Jack Yan]]. The Alliance stated its intention to run a list of candidates and electorate candidates in the 2008 general election. In April 2008 the party had between 500 and 600 members.[http://www.elections.org.nz/uploads/the_alliance.pdf Submission on distribution of broadcasting allocations]{{dead link|date=July 2017 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}, Alliance Party, 18 April 2008 During the process of regroupment since the 2005 election the Alliance has reaffirmed its role as a broad left-wing political party committed to contesting both electorate seats and a party list. The party continued to release an annual alternative budget, prepared by the Alliance spokesperson on tax, the academic and intelligence researcher [[Jim Flynn (academic)|Jim Flynn]]. In 2008 the Alliance adopted a new logo designed by Jack Yan & Associates{{cite web |url= http://jackyan.com/blog/2008/05/dressing-up-for-general-election-new.html |title=the Persuader Blog: Dressing up for the General Election: a new logo for the Alliance |publisher=Jack Yan |access-date=21 August 2014}} to signal the changes it has undergone and its intention for renewal and rebuilding. For the [[2008 New Zealand general election|2008 election]], the Alliance campaigned on stopping privatisation of public assets. It fielded candidates in all major New Zealand centres, contesting 15 electorate seats and running a party list of 30 candidates under the co-leaders Kay Murray and Andrew McKenzie. The party managed to marginally improve its party vote to 1,721, amounting to 0.08 percent of the party vote and placing the Alliance 7th out of 12 extra-parliamentary parties. The Alliance candidate for Dunedin North, Victor Billot, gathered 448 electorate votes, placing him 6th in that electorate. After the election of the fifth National government on 8 November 2008, the Alliance pledged to "play a leading role in resisting the attacks against public services, workers, beneficiaries and students that will be a feature of the new National Government."{{cite web|url=http://alliance.org.nz/2008/11/09/alliance-party-pledges-to-fight-for-public-interest/#more-702 |title=Party pledges to fight for public interest |publisher=Alliance |date=9 November 2008 |access-date=21 August 2014}} When Jim Anderton retired from politics in 2011, his [[Wigram (electorate)|Wigram]] electorate opened a potential route for the Alliance to return to Parliament. Former MP [[Kevin Campbell (New Zealand politician)|Kevin Campbell]] came out of retirement to contest the seat.{{Cite web |title=Former MP to contest Wigram for Alliance Party {{!}} Scoop News |url=https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PO1110/S00082/former-mp-to-contest-wigram-for-alliance-party.htm |access-date=2026-04-02 |website=www.scoop.co.nz}} Campbell only received 793 votes, placing him fourth, and the Alliance only received 1,069 party list votes, the lowest of any registered party.{{cite web |url=http://electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2011/partystatus.html |title=2011 Election Results – Overall Status |publisher=New Zealand Electoral Commission |access-date=27 November 2011 |archive-date=28 November 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111128232342/http://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2011/partystatus.html |url-status=dead }} It did not nominate a list for the [[2014 New Zealand general election|2014 election]], and nominated only a single electorate candidate: Mary O'Neill in [[Napier (New Zealand electorate)|Napier]] in which she came fifth with 59 votes.{{cite web |url=http://www.elections.org.nz/sites/default/files/plain-page/attachments/2014_electorate_candidates.xlsx |title=2014 Electorate Candidates |publisher=New Zealand Electoral Commission |date=27 August 2014 |access-date=27 August 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140827124622/http://www.elections.org.nz/sites/default/files/plain-page/attachments/2014_electorate_candidates.xlsx |archive-date=27 August 2014 |url-status=dead }} The party was formally deregistered with the [[Electoral Commission (New Zealand)|Electoral Commission]] at its own request on 26 May 2015. Without registration, the party cannot contest the party vote. In 2020, the former Alliance MP [[Phillida Bunkle]] wrote an essay for [[Newsroom (website)|''Newsroom'']] about her time in the party, in which she made allegations of a culture of bullying and misuse of funds, and of disruptive power-play by an internal grouping she called "the Faction."{{cite web |last1=Bunkle |first1=Phillida |title=Power and bullying: Parliament's ugly underside |url=https://www.newsroom.co.nz/politics/six-years-of-unrelenting-bullying-at-parliament |website=Newsroom |date=8 September 2020 |access-date=8 September 2020}} ===Relaunch=== In 2025, the party announced its intention to re-enter electoral politics by contesting the [[2025 New Zealand local elections]] in a press release. In the press release, party spokesperson Quentin Findlay claimed the party had experienced an influx of young membership.{{Cite web |date=1 June 2025 |title=The Return Of The Alliance 2025 – A Surprise Contender In Local Body Elections |url=https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/AK2506/S00003/the-return-of-the-alliance-2025-a-surprise-contender-in-local-body-elections.htm |access-date=3 June 2025 |website=[[Scoop (website)|Scoop]]}} As of June 2025, a new website had been launched for the party alongside the announcement.{{Cite web |title=Home |url=https://allianceparty.nz/ |access-date=3 June 2025 |website=Alliance Party |language=en-NZ}} Party president [[Victor Billot]] announced the party would contest a single seat at the [[2025 Christchurch City Council election]], Tom Roud in the [[Christchurch City Council]]'s central ward. Billot stated the party never fully disestablished but had been inactive for many years. Roud was unsuccessful, coming in fourth place with 407 votes.{{cite web |title=Christchurch City Council 2025 Triennial Elections – Declaration of Result |url=https://ccc.govt.nz/news-and-events/public-notices/show/1355 |publisher=[[Christchurch City Council]] |access-date=16 February 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260216095543/https://ccc.govt.nz/news-and-events/public-notices/show/1355 |archive-date=16 February 2026 |date=16 October 2025 |url-status=live}} In January 2026, the Alliance announced it will be standing electorate candidates in the [[2026 New Zealand general election]].{{cite news |author= |date= 21 January 2026 |title= Alliance Party: We Are Back To Fight For Working People In 2026 |url= https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PO2601/S00056/alliance-party-we-are-back-to-fight-for-working-people-in-2026.htm |website=[[Scoop (website)|Scoop]] |access-date= 30 January 2026 }} The party conference took place on 14 February 2026.{{Cite web |title=Alliance Party Prepares For 2026 General Election Campaign At Conference |url=https://m.scoop.co.nz/stories/PO2602/S00076/alliance-party-prepares-for-2026-general-election-campaign-at-conference.htm |access-date=2026-02-14 |website=[[Scoop (website)|Scoop]]}} In June 2026, the [[Maritime Union of New Zealand]] (MUNZ) national council unanimously voted to affiliate to the Alliance under Billot's leadership. He called it a "gamechanger" for that year's election and beyond for "advancing an uncompromising working class voice in New Zealand politics". MUNZ national secretary, Carl Findlay, said the union would also continue its long-standing affiliation with the Labour Party.{{cite news |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/597493/maritime-union-affiliates-with-alliance-party-keeps-door-open-to-labour |title=Maritime Union affiliates with Alliance Party, keeps door open to Labour |work=[[Radio New Zealand]] |date=7 June 2026 |access-date=9 June 2026 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20260609145759/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/597493/maritime-union-affiliates-with-alliance-party-keeps-door-open-to-labour |archive-date=9 June 2026|url-status=live}} A few days later, the party filed for re-registration.{{Cite web |date=12 June 2026 |title=Three parties apply to register |url=https://elections.nz/media-and-news/2026/three-parties-apply-to-register |access-date=12 June 2026 |website=[[Electoral Commission (New Zealand)|Electoral Commission]]}} The party was re-registered on 5 August 2026.{{cite web |url=https://elections.nz/media-and-news/2026/decisions-on-party-registrations-and-logos |title=Decisions on party registrations and logos |publisher=New Zealand Electoral Commission |date=5 August 2026 |access-date=5 August 2026}}{{cite web |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/election-2026-mariameno-kapa-kingis-new-party-approved-by-electoral-commission/DFSW2HKZVNDQZJPMGELK3NP3AY/ |title=Election 2026: Mariameno Kapa-Kingi’s new party approved by Electoral Commission |publisher=New Zealand Herald |author=Julia Gabel |date=5 August 2026 |access-date=6 August 2026}} ==Ideology and policy== At its foundation, the Alliance represented a big tent of politicians opposed to [[Rogernomics]] and [[Ruthanasia]]. While the main forces of the Greens and NewLabour were distinctly left-wing, the Liberals and Democrats were not and in the case of the latter, its centrist [[social credit]] economics were not reflected in the Alliance's policy.{{cite web |last1=Edwards |first1=Bryce |title=[NewLabour Party history] 18: Political differences within the Alliance |url=https://liberation.typepad.com/liberation/2009/05/newlabour-party-history-18-political-differences-within-the-alliance.html |website=liberation |access-date=4 July 2025 |date=29 May 2009}} Nevertheless, throughout the 1990s, the party presented itself as an anti-neoliberal, social democratic party (with democratic socialist factions) that emphasised workers' rights, green politics and free education and healthcare.{{cite web |title=Manifesto |url=http://www.alliance.org.nz/mani.htm |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/19970222064728/http://www.alliance.org.nz/mani.htm |archive-date=22 February 1997 |website=Alliance New Zealand}} In the coalition, they successfully introduced paid parental leave and KiwiBank. After moderate, pro-Labour faction left the party in 2002 to form the Progressive Coalition, the rump party under McCarten and Harré represented the trade union movement above all, focusing their 2002 campaign on extending paid leave to four weeks.{{cite web |date=1 May 2002 |title=Launch of Alliance campaign for four weeks annual leave |url=http://www.alliance.org.nz/info.php3?Type=Campaigns&ID=1065 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20021206164308/http://www.alliance.org.nz/info.php3?Type=Campaigns&ID=1065 |archive-date=6 December 2002 |access-date=4 July 2025}} In 2004, the party published a working manifesto that affirmed its commitment to socialism and collective ownership of the economy, a stance it retains to the present.{{Cite web |title=Alliance New Zealand |url= http://www.alliance.org.nz/ |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20040712042723/http://alliance.org.nz/policy/a5manifest.pdf |archive-date=12 July 2004}} In the mid-2000s, the party emphasised its opposition to capitalism altogether.{{Cite web |title=Alliance New Zealand |url=http://alliance.org.nz/info.php3?Type=Policy&ID=2112 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20051217172255/http://alliance.org.nz/info.php3?Type=Policy&ID=2112 |archive-date=2005-12-17 |access-date=2026-04-02 |website=alliance.org.nz}} In 2025, Victor Billot described the party as social democratic, but to the left of all other mainstream parties, while the party's official materials say it is committed to 'democratic socialism'.{{Citation |title=Alliance Party resurrects to contest Christchurch's central ward |first=Tina |last=Law |url=https://www.thepress.co.nz/nz-news/360716662/alliance-party-resurrects-contest-christchurchs-central-ward |work=[[The Press]] |date=10 June 2025 |access-date=10 June 2025 |language=en-NZ }} A democratic socialist party, the Alliance supports free [[education]], free [[healthcare]], [[full employment]] and the maintenance of the [[welfare state]]. Its policy platform emphasizes [[women's rights]], [[environmentalism]], and [[Māori people|Māori]] rights. It supports New Zealand's [[Nuclear-free zone|nuclear-free]] policy and opposes military interventionism, particularly during the [[War in Afghanistan (2001–present)|war in Afghanistan]]. The Alliance supports [[proportional representation]] for elections.{{cite web |url=http://alliance.org.nz/what-we-stand-for/alliance-policies/alliance-party-democracy-policy/ |title=Democracy |publisher=The Alliance |access-date=19 November 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714211511/http://alliance.org.nz/what-we-stand-for/alliance-policies/alliance-party-democracy-policy/|archive-date=14 July 2014 |quote=We stand for the following policies: * Proportional representation and a pluralist democratic system.}} The Alliance advocates a [[progressive tax]], which would mean a higher [[taxation|tax]] rate for wealthier people and a lower rate for poorer people. It also supports the removal of the [[Goods and Services Tax (New Zealand)|Goods and Services Tax]], seeing the tax as unfair because the amount paid does not vary according to the purchaser's ability to afford it; it advocates replacing this with a [[financial transaction tax]], or [[Tobin tax]]. ==Electoral results== ===National=== ====House of Representatives==== {| class=wikitable |- !
